title: sync/async/flush reset condition in lsu_cappuccino
body:
https://github.com/openrisc/mor1kx/blob/master/rtl/verilog/mor1kx_lsu_cappuccino.v#L524

``` verilog
always @(posedge clk)
     if (rst | pipeline_flush_i)
       atomic_reserve <= 0;
     else if (ctrl_op_lsu_store_i & ctrl_op_lsu_atomic_i & write_done ||
          !ctrl_op_lsu_atomic_i & store_buffer_write &
          (store_buffer_wadr == atomic_addr) ||
          (snoop_valid & (snoop_adr_i == atomic_addr)))
       atomic_reserve <= 0;
```

`(rst | pipeline_flush_i)` seems a bit dodgy if the timing tools were to analyse the net as an asyncronous reset (in other parts of the code) and synchronous here.  Maybe it's ok (who knows with fpga design tools!), though `pipeline_flush_i` could migrate, I think, to the first if condition and possibly a `OR_ASYNC_RST` added to the `always @` trigger.

title: [BUG] fcvt.s.d misses UF on boundary cases that round to the minimum normal single
body:
CVA6 reports incorrect fflags for a boundary fcvt.s.d case. The converted single-precision result matches Spike, but the underflow flag is missing.

I reproduced this on current master (02e11e3b9d9e6a087dc4811b933bf0cc80156e1a) with cv64a6_imafdc_sv39, using spike vs veri-testharness.

The minimal case is:

- input: 0x380fffffe0000000
- instruction: fcvt.s.d
- rounding mode: RNE

Both Spike and CVA6 produce the same final single-precision result:

But fflags differ:
- Spike: 0x03 (NX|UF)
- CVA6 RTL: 0x01 (NX)

Observed mismatch:
```
Mismatch[1]:
spike[1427] : pc[0000000080003020] csrrs   t2, fflags, zero: t2:0000000000000003
veri-testharness[1427] : pc[0000000080003020] csrrs   t2, fflags, zero: t2:0000000000000001
```

So this is not a wrong-result bug. The result value itself matches. The issue is that UF is not reported.

We suspect the RTL design file causing the error is fpnew_cast_multi.sv, where uf_after_round only checks whether the rounded exponent field is 0, missing the carry from denormal to min normal.

Minimal reproducer:
```
  .section .text
  .globl main
  main:
    li   t0, 0
    csrw frm, t0

    li   t0, 0x380fffffe0000000
    fmv.d.x ft0, t0

    csrw fflags, x0
    fcvt.s.d ft1, ft0
    fmv.x.w  t1, ft1
    csrr     t2, fflags

    li   a0, 0
    jal  exit
```

fix_commits.messageHeadline: fpnew_cast_multi: Fix underflow detection logic at subnormal-nomal

Thanks

@rgiunti @IhsaneTahir Thanks for the fix. I pulled the latest openhwgroup/cvfpu develop at 106251e502747f17d931a20db0bdbab9e1a6c2ff and reran my original CVA6 differential reproducer for issue #165.

Result: PASS. Spike and veri-testharness now agree on the boundary fcvt.s.d case:
```
  - input: 0x380fffffe0000000
  - instruction: fcvt.s.d
  - rounding mode: RNE
  - fflags: 0x03 (NX|UF) on both sides
```
So the issue looks resolved on my side.

Exactly the same UF flag missing bug in Xuantie C910 https://github.com/revyos/revyos/issues/47.

0077d9e buggy code before fix  commit cb3f0e5:

|                                    | Value                                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| **CEX input**                      | `0x380FFFFFD0000002` (RUP)                             |
| **FP64 true exponent**             | −127 = FP32 emin − 1 ✓                                 |
| **FP32 pre-round 23-bit fraction** | `0x7FFFFF` = all 23 bits 1 ✓                           |
| **Rounding action**                | `0x7FFFFF + 1 = 0x800000` → carry out → exponent 0 → 1 |
| **RTL result**                     | `0x00800000` (numerically correct)                     |
| **RTL fflags**                     | `0x01` (NX only — **UF missing**)                      |
| **Spec fflags**                    | `0x03` (NX\|UF — correct)                              |

### Exact the same cornel scene

1. **Condition 1** — exp of original result = emin−1 = −127 (FP32) ✓  
2. **Condition 2** — first N=23 explicit fraction bits all 1s (`0x7FFFFF`) ✓

title: Wrong assignment to enum variable from expression of different type
body:
Hey!
 Enum should be assignment only by enum type. LRM1800-2017 6.19.4: `A cast shall be required for an expression that is assigned to an enum variable where the type of the expression is not equivalent to the enumeration type of the variable.`
So in file ` design/ifu/ifu_ifc_ctl.sv` need to be change two lines:
`   assign next_state[1] = (~state[1] & state[0] & ~reset_delayed & miss_f2 & ~goto_idle) |
                          (state[1] & ~reset_delayed & ~mb_empty_mod & ~goto_idle);`
 for
`   assign next_state[1] = state_t'((~state[1] & state[0] & ~reset_delayed & miss_f2 & ~goto_idle) |
                          (state[1] & ~reset_delayed & ~mb_empty_mod & ~goto_idle));`

and
`   assign next_state[0] = (~goto_idle & leave_idle) | (state[0] & ~goto_idle) |
                          (reset_delayed);`
for
`   assign next_state[0] = state_t'((~goto_idle & leave_idle) | (state[0] & ~goto_idle) |
                          (reset_delayed));`
Like was done in pull request #49

comments.body: Thanks for reporting this, and #62. RTL will be fixed in the next release.

        wire	[3:0]  we_redund_3 = we & (addr[6:0] == 7'h1c) ? byteenable[3:0] : {4{1'b0}}; --> Line 54 in /v2.0/rev1/rtl/aib_avmm_io_csr.v

fix_commits.messageHeadline: issue #60 fix typo for redundancy control csr_shift_rxdat

comments.body:
Regarding 1. What you pointed out is true. **AIB[71]** is a typo. It should be AIB[73] instead for redundancy control enable.
Regarding 2. This is not a typo. Even though both are 7'h1c, we_tx_1 is 'h21C and we_redund_3 is 'h31C.

Thanks for pointing out the typo.  The correction has been checked in.

title: CJALR with instr[14:12] != 0 is not illegal
body:
The decoder for CJALR will not raise an illegal instruction exception when `instr[14:12] != 0`, but it will also not set `cheri_jalr_en`:

https://github.com/microsoft/cheriot-ibex/blob/3f0ec8600cb7621c4c952951d211b3515116ea27/rtl/ibex_decoder.sv#L343-L367

When a CJALR instruction is run with `instr[14:12] != 0`, the instruction that runs becomes one which stores the next instruction PC to the register file, but does not branch, since it runs into the old logic for JALR. This is therefore not a security issue, but is a bug.

Instead `illegal_insn` should be set when `instr[14:12] != 0` (see the original code for JALR, which does the same).

title: [BUG] Instruction fetch misaligned exception raised when a conditional branch that is not taken
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Hi,

According to the RISC-V 2.2 specification p.11: 
> An instruction address misaligned exception is generated on a taken branch or unconditional jump if the target address is not four-byte aligned. **No instruction fetch misaligned exception is generated for a conditional branch that is not taken**

But in `core/branch_unit.sv`, the exception is raised in branch unit as long as target address is misaligned *without taking the conditional branch result into account* :
`if (branch_valid_i && target_address[0] != 1'b0) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;` from [line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/72143ef0a9b50f2aaffa708a55263a5971bf0354/core/branch_unit.sv#L94) 

The fix should augment the `if` condition to include condition check that validate it is either an unconditional jump  or a **taken** conditional branch.


Thanks!

title: [Possible Issue] Non-selectable address matching mode leads to an incorrect PMP configuration update
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Instruction execution field `X`, and probably others, of PMP configuration CSRs is not updated correctly when trying to write non-selectable address matching value of field `A` in case PMP granularity `G` is `1`. Is this intended?

### RISC-V Specification
Unprivileged ISA: [20191213](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1s0lZxUZaa7eV_O0_WsZzaurFLLww7ou5/view) | Privileged Architecture: [20211203](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1EMip5dZlnypTk7pt4WWUKmtjUKTOkBqh/view) | External Debug Support: [0.13.02](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XSPqW3WIfflIMeuGJBxGTMOEyeuRAQ5F/view)
> The PMP configuration registers are densely packed into CSRs to minimize context-switch time.
For RV32, sixteen CSRs, pmpcfg0–pmpcfg15, hold the configurations pmp0cfg–pmp63cfg for the 64
PMP entries, as shown in Figure 3.31.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/09e7e476-c3a1-40c0-8a69-e2a59804d6f5)

> Figure 3.35 shows the layout of a PMP configuration register. The R, W, and X bits, when set,
indicate that the PMP entry permits read, write, and instruction execution, respectively. When
one of these bits is clear, the corresponding access type is denied. The R, W, and X fields form a
collectiveWARL field for which the combinations with R=0 and W=1 are reserved. The remaining
two fields, A and L, are described in the following sections.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/ca0ef0fb-261a-4e5d-a7ca-577121aa18ac)

> The A field in a PMP entry’s configuration register encodes the address-matching mode of the
associated PMP address register.

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/ec536bae-9b3f-4c48-90d4-4b555cf78c8e)

> Although the PMP mechanism supports regions as small as four bytes, platforms may specify
coarser PMP regions. In general, the PMP grain is 2G+2 bytes and must be the same across all
PMP regions. When G ≥ 1, the NA4 mode is not selectable.


### Example Scenario

As shown below, the following sequence of instructions happens: 
> CSRRS x0, pmp_cfg0, x1

The instruction `CSRRS x0, pmp_cfg0, x1` is decoded at `t_id` and executed in machine mode resulting in updating the architecture state at `t_arch_update`. As a result, instruction execution field `X` of `pmp3cfg` is not updated as expected. Where it's supposed to be set according to the written value of `x1`. Probably the reason for that is trying to write `NA4` value to the `A` field of the same register `pmp3cfg`, which is not selectable when the granularity `G` is `1`, and thus updating `A` is ignored correctly, but `X` has to be updated correctly still!

![Issue_15](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/872e3b2d-8c2d-4e2e-a45c-f111867ef021)

### Steps to Reproduce

Git Hash: [de2e254c](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/commit/de2e254cd4c2d3e3a6d4def1652918e8f2535512) | TARGET_CFG: [cv32a6_imac_sv0](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/include/cv32a6_imac_sv0_config_pkg.sv) | VCD: [issue_15.zip](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/files/14836579/issue_15.zip)

### Component
**Component:RTL**

---
Product: Questa OneSpin Solutions
App: Questa Processor App
Tool's version: 2024.1_1

title: [BUG] Wrong exception cause being raised in CSR Logic (illegal instruction instead of Virtual Instruction exception)
[BUG] An exploitable Meltdown vulnerability was found in CVA6
body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ### Bug Description Hi! Our processor side-channel vulnerability detection work has found an efficient and fault-tolerant Meltdown vulnerability on CVA6, which allows an attacker to leak kernel-space data at arbitrary addresses from user space. This vulnerability takes advantage of the feature of the CVA6 scoreboard: in-flight intructions in the scoreboard won’t trigger exceptions until they commit. Thus, we can access privilege data in a transient execution window and encode the privileged data in the microarchitecture. We provide an end-to-end exploit code and vulnerability explanation below. ```asm 2f40: fdiv.d fa5,fa5,fa4 2f44: lb t1, 0(a0) # a0 contains secret address 0xffffffffffe06f30, secret data is 0x30 2f48: slli t1, t1, 5 # encode secret to a probe array (index = secret << 5, t1 = 0x30 << 5 = 0x600) 2f4c: add t0, t1, t0 # encode secret to a probe array (base = 0x10000, t0 = base + t1 = 0x10600) 2f50: ld t1, 0(t0) # encode the secret to cache ``` The code runs under U-mode. The `lb` at `0x2f44` tries to access `0xffffffffffe06f30`, which is a kernel-space address. After the secret data is loaded, it will be encoded into the cache through the user-space array with the base address of `0x10000`. Due to the long latency of `fdiv` and the function [unit ready status](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L413), subsequent instructions will be issued during the `fdiv` transition execution window, as the waveform shows. **G1** represents the commit signals, **G2** represents scoreboard entries and **G3** represents the LSU, Dcache and memory bus behaviors. The first `lsu_valid_i` is triggered by `lb`, and the access address is successfully translated. The secret data is read from the Dcache and forwarded to the scoreboard. Thus, the `slli` and `add` can be issued in sequence. Finally, the secret is encoded in `t0`, which is the load address of` ld` at `0x2f50`. This is a cache-miss address. Thus, Dcache will fill the cacheline by initiating a memory access, as observed in `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`. All of the above processes take place within the `fdiv` transient execution window. In fact, when executing the `lb` at `0x2f44` architecturally, a load page fault exception will be triggered, and `t1` result will be 0. However, this is not important. We have already encoded the secret in the microarchitecture. Then we try to probe whether we successfully encoded the secret into the cache. The code sequentially accessed the memory addresses `0x105e0`, `0x10600`, `0x10620`, and `0x10640`. These addresses belong to different cachelines. ```asm probe: li t0, 0x10600 2f7c: ld t1, -32(t0) # cache miss 2f80: ld t1, 0(t0) # cache hit, addr = 0x10000 + 0x30 << 5 2f84: ld t1, 32(t0) # cache miss 2f88: ld t1, 64(t0) # cache miss ``` As shown in the waveform, compared with the `ld` that accesses `0x10600`, all the other `ld` have significantly longer execution times and all exhibit bus memory access behavior. Therefore, through the time side-channel, we can recover the aforementioned secret data. It is worth noting that this vulnerability has a high level of **fault tolerance**. Even if the secret address results in a TLB miss, this transient window is long enough to complete the Page Table Walk process. Similarly, if the address of the probe array also results in a TLB miss, the Page Table Walk can still be completed, and the secret can be encoded in the TLB. This vulnerability can be reproduced at the master commit aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd and the default cv64a6_imafdc_sv39 config. The full elf file are provided below. [rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24147141/rv64_test-av-CVA6-meltdown-fdiv.zip)

fix_commits.messageHeadline: fix forwarding results from instructions with exception (#3191)

comments.body:
Great work finding this vulnerability, and very well exposed.
A solution for this issue that comes to my mind is to not allow data that comes from a scoreboard entry with a valid exception to be forwarded. This could be done by adding a check on the forwarding mechanism in the issue_read_operands module, for instance. That way, instructions after `0x2f44` will not be executed.

Thank you @youssefekr for your kindly response and helpful advice! Your plan should be feasible and roughly consistent with what we had in mind. We are willing and are currently working on fixing it. I think we will PR later.

It seems this has been fixed by https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/pull/3191

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cvfpu/blob/8a18a8b468039c80f3988687009984f6299eb4d8/src/fpnew_divsqrt_th_64_multi.sv#L353-L354

fix_commits.messageHeadline: divsqrt_th_64: explicitly zero-extend operands to 64 bits

comments.body:
Hi @ricted98, thanks for catching this, this one is on me. I seem to have introduced this bug, when I fixed another one without realizing that `ct_vfdsu_top`'s ports are hardcoded to 64 bits. This slipped in simulation but was caught by synthesis elaboration.

I'll propose a fix that explicitly zero-extends the operands to 64 bits before connecting them to `ct_vfdsu_top`. Will follow up with a PR shortly.

Thanks @IhsaneTahir! The moment you have the PR I can test it again in my synthesis flow. I wanted to do the PR in the first place, but I was unsure about the correct way to extend the operands in this case.

title: Fix RAS
body:
Currently the RAS is left disconnected, yet some of the logic is synthesized when nRAS > 0.
https://github.com/riscv-boom/riscv-boom/blob/f35cc753a9cc5b15402cf7336f8a98912c6533a3/src/main/scala/bpu/bpd-pipeline.scala#L151-L152

This causes the vestigial RAS to inject false predictions to 0x0 in S1 of BTB, sometimes overriding the valid BTB predictions. In dhrystone MediumBoomConfig with a RAS takes 10% more cycles than SmallBoomConfig with no RAS. Preferably the RAS should be fixed and connected.

Side request: Can we also refactor the RAS to be a module, so that the internal registers and io is available to inspect in waveforms?

comments.body:
Is the performance bug mentioned above caused by RAS underflow? I just noticed that medium boom uses only 8 entries of RAS and turns off EmptyCheck. Because calling stack of dhrystone is deep, RAS underflow can degrade perfromance significantly.
My result shows that for small boom with 8-entry RAS, EmptyCheck boosts IPC for about 2%.
We found that for programs with a very shallow call stack, the RAS would mispredict more frequently than expected. There is some issue with the RAS update logic which is polluting it.

title: Should the default JTAG IDCODE be 0x1?
body:
https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/blob/9002e7e53299598027f41b95dba1666310923699/src/main/scala/rocketchip/DebugTransport.scala#L22

```scala
class JtagDTMKeyDefault extends JtagDTMConfig(
  idcodeVersion = 0,
  idcodePartNum = 0,
  idcodeManufId = 0,
debugIdleCycles = 5) // Reasonable guess for synchronization.
```

Should the default IDCODE be 0x1, or the same as in the previous debug module (0x10e31913)? Or should it throw an error message to prevent rocket from elaborating if the JTAG is enabled but the idcode is not specified?

@mwachs5 @palmer-dabbelt @ducky64

fix_commits.messageHeadline: Add a note to wire up jtag_mfr_id
Add a note to wire up jtag_mfr_id (#778)

comments.body:
The IDCODE (0x10e31913) uses SiFive's assigned JEDEC Manufacturer ID. So in general those who aren't SiFive should not be using that IDCODE. That's why we removed it from the default.

Those using rocket-chip repo should probably override this default value to something meaningful for their design. The ManufId is actually exported from the ExampleTop as part of its I/O and is tied off in the TestHarness.

I see, that makes sense. Thanks for the explanation. Would having an elaboration-time warning for users of rocket-chip be useful so that they don't run into surprises when they try to program their cores?

When you say "program their cores" do you mean when using OpenOCD to communicate with them? Is there actually a value that you use there that causes a problem? riscv-openocd is very tolerant of the IDCODE, it may print a warning if it's not the expected ID.

I'm not sure what the elaboration time warning would be because the mfr_id could go all the way out the pins of the chip. I added a runtime warning (so if you ran with simulate it could at least detect illegal idcodes, though the chances you detect an unconnected mfr_id are somewhat low):

https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/blob/master/src/main/scala/jtag/JtagTap.scala#L175

Note that if you did actually use the defaults here, then your IDCODE *would* be 0x1, because there is a bit in the IDCODE "always 1":
https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/blob/master/src/main/scala/rocketchip/DebugTransport.scala#L230

@mwachs5 Ah, I see. I think I see where my confusion was coming from now.

In https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/blob/9002e7e53299598027f41b95dba1666310923699/src/main/scala/rocketchip/DebugTransport.scala#L231 it uses two out of the three `Int`s in `JtagDTMConfig` but doesn't actually 
use the third one. I was confused since I thought that all 3 would be determined at elaboration-time by `JtagDTMConfig`. In my design, I think I left io.jtag_mfr_id unconnected and the synthesis tool tied it at some point to zero.

Perhaps if we are not actually going to use `c.idcodeManufId.U`, perhaps it could be a good idea to put in a comment saying "Please wire up io.jtag_mfr_id to set the mfr_id or something"? The TestHarness I think manually goes and re-retrieves it (or maybe just remove `idcodeManufId` from `JtagDTMConfig` to avoid confusion perhaps).

```scala
  idcode.always1    := 1.U
  idcode.version    := c.idcodeVersion.U
  idcode.partNumber := c.idcodePartNum.U
  idcode.mfrId := io.jtag_mfr_id
```

The comment seems like a reasonable request. Keep in mind that RocketChipExampleTop is just an example top level, and other designs could actually wire up mfrId using the value in JtagDTMConfig,  I think we should leave it there but comment it as you suggest.
Thoughts on https://github.com/freechipsproject/rocket-chip/pull/778 ?

title: Litex SoC binds to non-existent ports when generating a NaxRiscv-based SoC with --with-jtag-instruction
body:
Hello,

# Issue
I'm trying to implement a NaxRiscv-based SoC on FPGA (Digilent Genesys 2) but synthesis fails, as the SoC's top level module instantiating the Nax tries to connect to port which do not exist.

Precisely, I'm trying to add a JTAG debug module within the Nax, which thus exposes I/O ports in the Nax's top level. For some reason, when integrating the Nax in the SoC's top level, Litex seems to detect different signal names for the JTAG ports, than the ones actually exposed by the Nax, which thus causes an error during synthesis.


Instantation of the NaxRiscv in the SoC top module (namely the verilog file ```build/gateware/digilent_genesys2.v```)
```verilog
//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Instance NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 of NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 Module.
//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934(
        /* Remaining ports connections */
        .jtag_instruction_capture           (basesoc_jtag_capture),
        .jtag_instruction_clk               (basesoc_jtag_clk),
        .jtag_instruction_enable            (basesoc_jtag_enable),
        .jtag_instruction_reset             (basesoc_jtag_reset),
        .jtag_instruction_shift             (basesoc_jtag_shift),
        .jtag_instruction_tdi               (basesoc_jtag_tdi),
        .jtag_instruction_update            (basesoc_jtag_update),
        /* Remaining ports connections */
       	);
```

Definition of the NaxRiscv top module
```verilog
module NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 (
	/* Remaining ports declaration */
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_tdi,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_enable,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_capture,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_shift,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_update,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_reset,
	output wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_tdo,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_clk
	/* Remaining ports declaration */
);
	/* RTL */
endmodule
```

As one can see from the above RTL snippets, except for ```jtag_instruction_clk``` which is correct, JTAG signals are declared with prefix ```jtag_instruction_instruction``` whilst the SoC is mapping to ports with prefix ```jtag_instruction```.

# Build options

comments.body:
Hello @benjaminh-13,

I suggest 2 solutions: 

- either make a modification on the NaxRiscv side, 
- or make a modification on the Litex side.

#### On the NaxRiscv side

You'll need to modify the file that generates the SoC for Litex, NaxSoc, by changing this line :

https://github.com/SpinalHDL/NaxRiscv/blob/43716b5770e8ac689e9778056c061da577dcf17e/src/main/scala/naxriscv/platform/litex/NaxSoc.scala#L209

by this one : 

```scala
if (withJtagInstruction) debug.instruction.setName("jtag")
```

What happens is that the string `jtag_instruction` is added to the variable name `instruction` in [DebugModuleFiber](https://github.com/SpinalHDL/SpinalHDL/blob/af8fab4da5a73c785c4f2e2f68af2c9b34fd6aec/lib/src/main/scala/spinal/lib/cpu/riscv/debug/DebugModuleFiber.scala#L95) when the verilog is generated.

So to change the name of the totality, another way would be as follows :

```scala
if (withJtagInstruction) debug.instruction.instruction.setName("jtag_instruction")
```

#### On the Litex side

You need to modify the core.py file associated with NaxRiscv.

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/48e65c199de6bd1d5aead61d7f515356cc7ecab8/litex/soc/cores/cpu/naxriscv/core.py#L428-L437

You need to update the assignments with the “jtag_instruction_instruction” prefix.

```python
self.cpu_params.update(
    i_jtag_instruction_clk     = self.jtag_clk,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_enable  = self.jtag_enable,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_capture = self.jtag_capture,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_shift   = self.jtag_shift,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_update  = self.jtag_update,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_reset   = self.jtag_reset,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_tdi     = self.jtag_tdi,
    o_jtag_instruction_instruction_tdo     = self.jtag_tdo,
)
```

After one of these two modifications, the Vivado synthesis should work.

Best regards

Hello @atkarim,

Thank you for the very quick response.

I tried solution 2, namely bringing changes to the NaxRiscv's ```core.py``` in Litex and now synthesis succeeds. As a consequence, I am closing this issue.

Thanks again,
Best regards,

title: Cache performance will degrade in some simulator due to the implement of module "cache_lru"
body:
Recently I have managed to port the Nyuzi to Xilinx ZC706 evaluation board and run doom & quakeview successfully, with respect. But during this process, I noticed a cache performance degradation when debugging with Modelsim SE 10.5c. Since such degradation seems only existing when simulating in some simulators and doesn't exist in verilator or after synthesize, I think maybe this topic is more like a portability suggestion than an issue.

When running the core on some simulators such as Modelsim, the x value coming from uninitialized SRAM will cause the casez statement in module cache_lru fail to match any pattern, further cause that in all cache set only way 0 is available. To illustrate it clearly, here is a piece of code snipping from cache_lru.sv when parameter NUM_WAYS is 4.

```
...

#130            4:
#131            begin
#132                always_comb
#133                begin
#134                    casez (lru_flags)
#135                        3'b00?: fill_way = 0;
#136                        3'b10?: fill_way = 1;
#137                        3'b?10: fill_way = 2;
#138                        3'b?11: fill_way = 3;
#139                        default: fill_way = '0;
#140                    endcase
#141                end
#142
#143                always_comb
#144                begin
#145                    case (new_mru)
#146                        2'd0: update_flags = {2'b11, lru_flags[0]};
#147                        2'd1: update_flags = {2'b01, lru_flags[0]};
#148                        2'd2: update_flags = {lru_flags[2], 2'b01};
#149                        2'd3: update_flags = {lru_flags[2], 2'b00};
#150                        default: update_flags = '0;
#151                    endcase
#152                end
#153            end

...
```

Consider after reset, two or more cache fill operations happened in the same cache set. When the first fill request comes, because the value of "lru_flags" is 3'bxxx (the value of uninitialized SRAM), the default branch will take effect, way 0 got filled, and the "update_flags" will be 3'b11x. Then, in the subsequent request handling process, the casez statement will always fail to match any pattern with the value of "lru_flags" (3'b11x), the default branch will always take effect, way 0 will always get filled, and "update_flags" will always be 3'b11x. The similar issue also exists when NUM_WAY is 8. The marked red area in the waveform generated by Modelsim attached below shows such situation:

![lru_waveform](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25722008/1ba40f0e-3145-11e7-93f3-f02092e1a397.png)

Although it sounds like a bad idea, one solution to this problem is changing all casez in cache_lru.sv to casex. I made an experiment to estimate the performance impact: Some logic was inserted into the writeback_stage firstly to trace the function activity. Then, the same program got executed on two different designs, the original design and the design with modified cache_lru, for a given time. Since the program is same, the amount of log generated during simulation is related to the instructions got executed. By comparing the number of function tracing record, we can compare the performance approximately. The screenshot below shows the result: The design with modified cache_lru produced 2.8x more log than the original one, which can roughly be considered as running faster 2.8x.

![log](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25721242/4dfccdae-3142-11e7-8a54-6c918b5deaa7.png)

The version I use is ce221ff, but this issue still exists in the latest version.

Finally, Thanks for bringing such interesting project!

![img_20170502_233302](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25722013/219d087a-3145-11e7-8ea3-75685d58b288.jpg)

comments.body:
Good catch! Nice write up of the issue too, thanks.

Since Verilator is only a two-state simulator (no x or z), it doesn't manifest this problem, but any four-state simulator probably will. Another solution might be to initialize the SRAMs to 0 at startup.
This patch should address the issue, but feel free to let me know if not.

Sadly, if a logic/reg variable is driven in an always_ff block, the "vlog" compiler in the latest Modelsim seems doesn't allow any other block drive that single again, even it's an initial block. So the patch 7780328 just can't pass the compile. 

![compile_error](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8781507/25739227/95386798-31b3-11e7-8bb9-f494bdeacd1e.png)


The following patch is ok with the help of macro SIMULATION, but not very beautiful...

+++ sram_1r1w_patched.sv        2017-05-05 16:32:46.063266600 +0800
@@ -100,7 +100,11 @@

+`ifdef SIMULATION
+    always @(posedge clk)
+`else

+`endif

@@ -120,6 +124,11 @@

+`endif
+
         if ($test$plusargs("dumpmems") != 0)

```

```
--- sram_2r1w_ce221ff.sv        2017-03-22 23:48:00.614532400 +0800
+++ sram_2r1w_patched.sv        2017-05-05 16:32:48.783422200 +0800
@@ -128,7 +128,11 @@

Yeah, a bit hacky, but I'm not sure of another way to do this cleanly now. Pushed another patch.

I didn't add the SIMULATION guards in this patch. Did you need that because you are inferring the SRAM for the Xilinx part in that block? I would have expected the last block to not infer SRAMs properly (with an area and clock speed hit), but perhaps this works okay on Xilinx.  It definitely doesn't on Altera. I *think* it might be preferable to have a VENDOR_XILINX block and explicitly instantiate the block RAM, like how it is done in VENDOR_ALTERA, to avoid any issues.

Yes, currently the SRAM in my design is inferred from this block because it just works... Thanks for the advice. I will make a VENDOR_XILINX block and submit a pull request after finished.

title: [BUG] Out-of-Order Not Working
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

## Bug Explanation

I noticed the docs say that Out-of-Order can occur between the multiplier and the ALU, however this is not the case according to the RTL.

Docs:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/a29b231070f2dccca53eae2681120116633a4ffc/docs/03_cva6_design/issue_stage.md?plain=1#L42-L54

RTL:

https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/adf99b53042d2b14cbbb36689babf8cd4c03cf81/core/issue_read_operands.sv#L135-L152

For example, I have this code snippet:

```
        div     t2, t0, t1
        fsqrt.s f1, f1
        lw      t5, 0(s1)
        add     t6, t0, t1
```

And this is it's execute stage:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/43790149/223483191-73f6885e-c1e1-4930-bf28-4377288d72b6.png)

As you can see, the `add` instruction isn't run until after the `div` finishes.

## Proposed Fix

Either:

* The RTL could be changed to separate the ALU and multiplier into two separate busy signals.
* The example in the docs could be changed to something else, such as `div` and `lsu`.

docs: fix example of OoO write-back to scoreboard (#1621)

comments.body: If you like, I can submit a pull request changing the docs to give div and lsu as the example

Hello @sifferman and thanks for opening this issue.

I had a look, I think I have found a too strict restriction (#1230) related to `mult -> *` sequences. However it does not seem to fix this issue about `div -> flu` sequences.

The parallelism is only possible for units spread on different result buses, so that their result can be provided to the scoreboard without conflicts. For the `div -> add` sequence you show, they use the same result bus (named `flu` as "fixed latency unit", even if div does not have a fixed latency), so you are right, the doc example is wrong.

A few suggestions/ideas:

- We can update the docs as you suggest.
- We could add a write-back port for `mult/div` but we won't as the area cost would be considerable!
- We can check if there is a minimal latency for div; if so, maybe we could issue a few other FLU instructions just after the `div` starts?
- Maybe we could modify how the div result is handled: when div result is available, if result bus is available then push the result, else store it in a (new?) register and lock the `flu` issues until the result bus is available, then release the lock and push the result.
- Maybe we could move the `mult/div` unit to the same port as FP operations?

Thanks for taking a look @cathales! I agree with your observations.

Actually, I believe that the throughput could increase quite a bit if the mult/div unit uses the FP port. On a mult/div instruction, it's probably more likely that the next instruction will be an ALU instruction than a FPU instruction. But I'm not sure how big of an endeavor it would be to complete this.

I will have time to look into it in about a month if progress hasn't been made on it sooner

If we move mult/div to FP port, I hope multiply-accumulate would not need bubbles anymore if the compiler is smart enough to avoid RAW hasards like below:

```asm
mul m0, a, b
; begin repeat
mul m1, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m0 ; now: bubble because same bus than previous mul -> after modification: issue ok
mul m0, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m1 ; bubble -> issue ok
; end repeat
add r, r, m0 ; issue ok
```

However, if the compiler does not do that (see below), there will be the same bubbles anyway so the modification will not impact performance.

```asm
; begin repeat
mul m, a, b ; issue ok
add r, r, m ; bubble because needs m from mul above and mul duration is 2 cycles
; end repeat
````

> Actually, I believe that the throughput could increase quite a bit if the mult/div unit uses the FP port. On a mult/div instruction, it's probably more likely that the next instruction will be an ALU instruction than a FPU instruction. But I'm not sure how big of an endeavor it would be to complete this.

For CoreMark the increase would be less than 3%, but it depends of the application.

About area:

For a configuration with both F and M, we use an existing write-back port so it is okay.

For a configuration with M, without F, today there should not be a write-back port for FPU, so the muxes in the scoreboard could be cheap. If we add one port for the multiplier, it means that the muxes are big.

So maybe the performance vs area cost should be discussed.

title: [BUG] About four-byte alignment on target addresses of control transfer instructions (branch_unit.sv)
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Hi,
 
In `core/branch_unit.sv` the `branch_exception_o.valid` is raised high only if the branch/jump target address is not aligned **on a two-byte boundary** ([line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/513bb91f823a18a6653a1685acd60408049c9c8f/core/branch_unit.sv#L94C8-L96C10) checks only the LSB). That is, it enforces only two-byte boundary check, and does not raise exception when target address of JAL/JALR is not four-byte aligned. 
However, in RISC-V 2.1 specification p.16 says "The JAL and JALR instructions can generate a misaligned instruction fetch exception if the target address is not aligned to a four-byte boundary."

If my understanding is correct, I think the fix may need to change the condition of [line 94](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/513bb91f823a18a6653a1685acd60408049c9c8f/core/branch_unit.sv#L94C8-L96C10) from. 
`if (branch_valid_i && target_address[0] != 1'b0) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;` to   
`if (branch_valid_i && (target_address[1:0] != 2'b00)) branch_exception_o.valid = 1'b1;`

Thanks!

title: Previous privilege mode mstatus field MPP holds reserved value
body:
### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing bug issues

### Bug Description

Previous privilege mode field, `MPP`, of `mstatus` or `sstatus` holds reserved value. The example where this applies to `sstatus` is not shown here.

### RISC-V Specification
Unprivileged ISA: [20191213](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1s0lZxUZaa7eV_O0_WsZzaurFLLww7ou5/view) | Privileged Architecture: [20211203](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1EMip5dZlnypTk7pt4WWUKmtjUKTOkBqh/view) | External Debug Support: [0.13.02](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XSPqW3WIfflIMeuGJBxGTMOEyeuRAQ5F/view)
> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/b6ee3012-d5e7-4f99-94c9-0cb40737aa43)

> ![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/20941d38-bc11-4436-96b2-8ae3dfcaf8c6)


### Example Scenario

As shown below, the following sequence of instructions happens: 
> CSRRW x2, mstatus, x9 -> CSRRCI x1, mstatus, 0

The instruction `CSRRW x2, mstatus, x9` is decoded at `t_id` and executed in machine mode resulting in updating the architecture state at `t_arch_update`. As a result, a wrong value of the `MPP` field of `mstatus` is read considering that it's a reserved one.

![Issue_12](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/28307467/15258d6e-f2f0-4933-a000-a6eb61514b9f)

### Steps to Reproduce

Git Hash: [de2e254c](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/commit/de2e254cd4c2d3e3a6d4def1652918e8f2535512) | TARGET_CFG: [cv32a6_imac_sv0](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/include/cv32a6_imac_sv0_config_pkg.sv) | VCD: [issue_12.zip](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/files/14826417/issue_12.zip)

Hello, 
this is a RTL bug in the cva6 [Decoder](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/decoder.sv), the problem appears in this code 
![image](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/assets/110232072/225efdd5-2fa1-48e2-9665-f728ed32c501)

Hi @cfuguet,

I encountered an issue while running tests for the target `cv64a6_imafdc_sv39_hpdcache` with the HPD-Cache configured in write-back mode. Below are the steps and observations:

### Steps to Enable Write-Back Mode
To enable write-back mode, I modified the following parameters in the file `core/cache_subsystem/cva6_hpdcache_subsystem.sv`:

```Shell
flushEntries: 4,
flushFifoDepth: 2,
wtEn: 1'b0,
wbEn: 1'b1
```

    - `riscv-arch-test-cv64a6_imafdc_sv39`

Tests with **virtual memory enabled** (e.g., `riscv-tests-cv64a6_imafdc_sv39-v`) fail. The simulation crashes within the design of the Verilator model, leading to a timeout.

### Example Failure

comments.body:
Hello @Bill94l, thank you for reporting the issue.

I will take a look on it, and let you know.

As you can see, the write-back mode of the HPDcache is not yet officially supported on the CVA6 as there is no a corresponding configuration, so you may have some issues. But anyway, It should in principle work.

Ok, I diagnosed the issue but I did not yet fixed it. It is not a very simple one. It is an integration bug: hpdcache in WB mode within the CVA6.

It is a cache coherency issue between the Icache and the Dcache (HPDcache). The runtime in the v-tests (tests with virtual memory), modifies instruction segments. These modifications are done locally in the HPDcache (because of the write-back mode), and are not visible by the instruction cache unless the HPDcache is flushed (this is not required when in write-through mode because the memory is always updated on writes). The runtime explicitly does this using a fence.i instruction, but currently this instruction only requests an invalidation of the Icache with no flush of the Dcache.

I need to modify the CVA6 controller to issue a CMO flush operation to the HPDCache in case of a fence.i instruction, or find another clever way to keep both caches coherent... I have some ideas but I will think it over a little more.

You will need to be a little patient for this one.

Hi @Bill94l,

The fix is on its way. I have an opened Pull Request #2691 that fixes the coherency issue between the Icache and the Dcache when using the HPDcache in WB mode.

title: [BUG] Spectre-type Vulnerability and Its Different Variants were Found in CVA6
body: ### Is there an existing CVA6 bug for this? - [x] I have searched the existing bug issues ## Summary We creatively used `ecall` to delay the resolution of the branch, creating a branch misprediction transient window. In this window, we can access kernel-space data and encode it in different microarchitecture components at U-mode without exception. ## Bug Description Hi! Our processor side-channel vulnerability detection work has found Spectre vulnerability and its different variants on CVA6, which allows an attacker to leak kernel-space data from user space without exception. CVA6 employs thie Scoreboard for out-of-order issuing. The Scoreboard algorithm won't issue instructions that have RAW conflicts. Therefore, when a B-type instruction is issued, its operands are already ready. So, B-type instructions can be resolved very quickly. As a result, the traditional Spectre vulnerabilities cannot perform the secret access and encoding operation within the CVA6's 1-2 cycles branch midprediction window. However, we creatively introduce `ecall` to delay the resolution of the branch. `ecall` is a instruction that will implicitly write register `a0`. But in the implementation of CVA6 Scoreboard, `ecall` won't be in conflict with the subsequent instructions that take `a0` as an operand. This give us a chance to issue B-type instruction with operand `a0`. CVA6 will read the old value of `a0` and make a wrong descision on the B-type instrucion. Then, we accessed and encoded the secret on the wrong branch. This takes advantage of the feature of the CVA6 Scoreboard: in-flight intructions in the scoreboard won’t trigger exceptions until they commit, which we have illustrated in detail in previous issue: [An exploitable Meltdown vulnerability was found in CVA6](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/issues/3163). We provide an end-to-end exploit code and vulnerability explanation below. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall # overwrite a0 to a non-zero value 2f48: bnez a0, 2f84 # the old value of a0 is zero 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 0xffffffffffe04000 2f50: slli t0, t0, 0x5 # use secret as index 2f54: add t0, t1, t0 # t1 contains probe array address 0x10000 2f58: ld t1, 0(t0) # encode secret to probe array ... 2f84 : # the true control flow will jump to here ... ``` The code runs under U-mode. `a0` is initialized to 0. The `lb` at `0x2f4c` tries to access `0xffffffffffe04000`, which is a kernel-space address. After the secret data is loaded, it will be encoded into the cache through the user-space array with the base address of `0x10000`. Due to the long latency of fdiv and the misprediction of `bnez`, subsequent instructions will be issued during the transition execution window, as the waveform shows. **G1** represents the [commit signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/scoreboard.sv#L100).**G2** represents [Scoreboard entries](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/scoreboard.sv#L100). **G3** represents the LSU, Dcache and memory bus behaviors, including [`lsu_valid_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L52), [`vaddr_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L575), [`paddr_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/load_store_unit.sv#L579), [`miss_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/wt_dcache.sv#L37), [`mem_rtrn_vld_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/wt_dcache.sv#L51), `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`, `io_axi4_0_ar_bits_addr` and `io_axi4_0_r_valid`. The first `lsu_valid_i` is triggered by `lb`, and the access address is successfully translated. The secret data is read from the Dcache and forwarded to the Scoreboard. Thus, the `slli` and `add` can be issued in sequence. Finally, the secret is encoded in `t0`, which is the load address of `ld` at `0x2f58`. This is a cache-miss address. Thus, Dcache will fill the cacheline by initiating a memory access, as observed in `io_axi4_0_ar_valid`. All of the above processes take place within the `fdiv` transient execution window. After `ecall` trap process finished, `a0` will be modified to a non-zero value. `bnez` at `0x2f48` will taken and control flow will skip these instructions between `0x2f4c` and `0x2f58`. But these instructions have been microarchitecturally executed. Then we try to probe whether we successfully encoded the secret into the cache. The code sequentially accessed the memory addresses `0x10000`, `0x10010`, `0x10020`, and `0x10030`. These addresses belong to different cachelines. ``` 5000: lui t0, 0x10 5004: ld t1, 0(t0) # t0 = 0x10000 5008: ld t1, 16(t0) 500c: ld t1, 32(t0) 5010: ld t1, 48(t0) ``` As shown in the waveform, compared with the `ld` that accesses `0x10020`, all the other `ld` have significantly longer execution times and all exhibit bus memory access behavior. Therefore, through the time side-channel, we can recover the aforementioned secret data. This vulnerability can be reproduced at the master commit [aa4f5a5](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/commit/aa4f5a548b33f7edff63483347fc8510aa9ad5fd) and the default cv64a6_imafdc_sv39 config. The full elf file are provided below. ## Variants In CVA6, not only the DCache can be used as a component for encoding and decoding secrets. We have discovered that the frontend states, such as BTB, BHT, RAS, etc., can be changed within the transient window. And after the speculation execution was rolled back, these states will not be rolled back. Thus, secrets can be encoded in these front-end components. ### BTB [BTB](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L28) is a frontend branch prediction unit. It provides branch prediction for `jalr` instructions except for `call` and `ret`. BTB will record the target addresses of these `jalr` instructions, and when it encounters the corresponding `jalr` again in the future, it will directly predict the jump address to be the recorded target address. As shown in the following code, we have constructed a jump address that depends on the secret. Depending on the secret, the target address for the `jalr` instruction located at `0x2f58` will change. During the transient window, after the `jalr` target jump address is calculated, the BTB entries will be updated. After the transient window rollback, the BTB entries will not be invalidated, so we will keep the secret in the BTB. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 80002f9c 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: slli t0, t0, 0x2 2f54: add t1, t1, t0 # t1 contains probe address 2f58 : 2f58: jalr t0, t1 # train the btb, different secret will reseult in different target address ... 2f8c : 2f8c: nop 2f90: nop 2f94: nop 2f98: nop ... ``` As shown in the following two waveform figures. We changed the value of secret and ran the testcase. When the secret is 0, the predicted jump address of the corresponding entry in the BTB will be updated to `2f8c`. When the secret is 1, the predicted jump address of the corresponding entry in the BTB will be updated to `2f90`. **G5** represents [BTB update signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L45). **secret = 0** **secret != 0** Next, we will attempt to decode the data. Based on the analysis of the [BTB entry matching mechanism](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L69), we found that BTB makes predictions only based on the lower bits of the PC, and does not match the entire PC. Therefore, we use the following instruction for decoding. ``` 5000: la t1, probe # t1 = 0x2f8c ... 5058: jalr t0, t1 ``` During the decoding stage, we placed a `jalr` instruction at the address `0x5058`. This address shares the same BTB entry with the `jalr` instruction that previously encoded the secret at `0x2f58`. So it will trigger branch prediction. **G4** represents [BTB prediction signals](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/btb.sv#L47). If the secret is 0, then the branch prediction is correct and the execution time is shorter. If the secret is 1, then the branch prediction is incorrect and the execution time will be slower. So this creates a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### BHT [BHT](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv) is also a frontend branch predictor. It records the jump situations of the B-type instructions. When it encounters the corresponding B-type instructions again, it makes branch prediction based on the recorded historical information. This BHT uses a 2-bit [saturation counter](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L56) to record the historical taken/untaken situations. If a B-type instruction is taken, the saturation counter of the corresponding entry is incremented by one. When the value of the saturation counter is greater than or equal to 2, it predicts that the B-type instruction will be taken in the future. We conduct the following testcase. The `beqz` instruction at `0x2f50` is taken/untaken based on whether the secret is zero. We use this instruction to encode the secret. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2f80 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: 2f50: beqz t0, 2f7c # train BHT ... 2f7c : ``` The two waveform diagrams below illustrate the encoding stages under different secrets. **G5** represents the [BHT entry](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L59) corresponding to the `beqz` instruction. When the secret is 0, the `beqz` instruction is taken and updates the corresponding saturation counter to 1. When the secret is 1, the `beqz` instruction is untaken, and the saturation counter for the corresponding entry remains unchanged and stays at 0. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We use the following instructions to decode the secret. Similar to BTB, BHT also only matches the lower bits of the PC to determine a BHT entry. We placed a `beqz` instruction at the address `0x5050`. This instruction will use the same BHT entry as the `beqz` instruction that encodes secret at address `0x2f50`. We set `t0` to 0 so that the `beqz` instruction will be taken. Then we observe the behavior of the `beqz` instruction at address 0x5050 at its second time execution. ``` 5000: li t0, 0 ... 5050: beqz t0, 5000 ``` **G4** represents the [BHT prediction result](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/bht.sv#L42) for the `beqz` instruction at address `0x5050`. When the secret is 0, this BHT entry records two branch takens. Therefore, when the instruction at `0x5050` is executed for the second time, the BHT will predicte it to be taken. The branch prediction is correct and the execution time is faster. When the secret is 1, this BHT entry records only one branch taken. The BHT will predicte it to be untaken. The branch prediction is incorrect and the execution time slows down. This forms a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### RAS [RAS](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv) is used to push the return address onto the stack when making a call. We attempted to utilize RAS to create a temporal side-channel. By performing secret-dependent RAS operations within the transient window, the secret is encoded within the RAS. After the transient window rollback, the status of RAS will not be revoked. This enables the decoding of the secret. In the following testcase, `ra` is influenced by the secret. If the secret is 0, then the `jalr` instruction located at `0x2f58` will be executed. Executing this instruction will push the address of the next instruction into RAS, thereby changing the state of RAS. If the secret is not zero, then `0x2f58` will be skipped and the state of RAS will not be changed. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5,fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2fb0 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) # a1 contains secret address 2f50: add ra, t2, t0 # t2 is initialized to 0x2f58. RAS top = previous call address + 4 2f54: ret # pop RAS. if t0 == 0, continue to execute 0x2f58 2f58: jalr ra, t3 # push 0x2f5c into RAS. RAS top = 0x2f5c ``` **G4** represents the RAS-related signal. Including the push signal [`push_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L29), the data pushed onto the stack [`data_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L33), the pop signal [`pop_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L31), the valid signal indicating the availability of the top stack data [`data_o.valid`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L35), and the data at the top of the stack [`data_o.ra`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/frontend/ras.sv#L35). When the secret is 0, the `jalr` instruction at `0x2f58` within the transient window is executed, pushing `0x2f5c` into the stack. When the secret is not 0, the state of RAS has not changed. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We use the following code to decode the secret. We execute an instruction that returns to `0x2f5c`. At this point, RAS is used for target address prediction. This address is precisely the value that was pushed into RAS when the secret was 0. ``` 5000: li ra, 0x2f5c 5008: ret ``` Observe the ret instruction located at 0x5008. If the value of "secret" is 0, the prediction is correct and the execution time is fast. If the value of "secret" is not 0, the prediction will be incorrect and the execution time will be slow. This forms a timing side-channel. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ### ICache All the instructions executed by CVA6 come from the [ICache](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv). The reading of instructions is strongly related to the control flow. So we attempted to influence the control flow through "secret", thereby affecting the state of the ICache, in order to encode the secret into the ICache. In the following testcase, a secret-dependent `beqz` instruction was placed at the address `0x2f50`. If the secret is 0, it will jump to the `probe` instruction block. It is necessary to ensure beforehand that the `probe` instruction block is not in the ICache. ``` 2f40: fdiv.d fa5, fa5, fa4 2f44: ecall 2f48: bnez a0, 2f90 2f4c: lb t0, 0(a1) 2f50: beqz t0, 2f80 ... 2f80 : ``` **G4** represents the signals related to the ICache, including the ICache miss signal [`miss_o`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv#L50) and the instructions request signal [`areq_i`](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cva6/blob/master/core/cache_subsystem/cva6_icache.sv#L52). When the secret is 0, the control flow needs to jump to the `probe` instruction block at address `0x2f80`. Since the `probe` instruction is not located in the ICache, an ICache miss occurred. At this point, the ICache initiates a refill request to the memory. Ultimately, the content of the `probe` instruction block is filled back into the ICache. However, when the secret is not zero, the `probe` instruction block will not be filled into the ICache. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** We directly execute the probe instruction block and observe the execution time. ``` 5000: j 2f80 ``` It can be observed that when the secret is 0, the `probe` instruction block has already been loaded into the ICache during the transient window, so when jumping to the `probe` instruction block, it can be executed directly. However, when the secret is not zero, the `probe` instruction block will not be loaded in the transient window. Thus, an ICache miss occurs and the instruction needs to be fetched from the memory, resulting in a significant time difference. **secret = 0** **secret != 0** ## Conclusion Overall, although CVA6 uses the scoreboard for instruction scheduling and inherently has a relatively small transient execution window, it can still be bypassed in various ways. Moreover, the microarchitecture of CVA6 has numerous timing vulnerabilities. [CVA6-spectre-ecall-dcache.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755549/CVA6-spectre-ecall-dcache.zip) [CVA6-spectre-ecall-btb.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755552/CVA6-spectre-ecall-btb.zip) [CVA6-spectre-ecall-bht.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755554/CVA6-spectre-ecall-bht.zip) [CVA6-spectre-ecall-icache.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755556/CVA6-spectre-ecall-icache.zip) [CVA6-spectre-ecall-ras.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24755557/CVA6-spectre-ecall-ras.zip)

title: PoR value of MSTATUS
body:
### Bug Description

The [documented](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cve2/blob/b8c94a3e84087e230581fcdddadbea398ea19a7e/doc/03_reference/cs_registers.rst?plain=1#LL109C1-L109C1) power-on-reset value of the `mstatus` CSR (0x300) is 0x0000_1800 which expands to:

| Bit Pos  | PoR | Field     |
| ------- | ----- | -------------- |
| 21    | 1'b0  | **TW**  |
| 17    | 1'b0 | **MPRV**  |
| 12:11 | 2'b11  | **MPP**  |
| 7     | 1'b0  | **MPIE** |
| 3     | 1'b0  | **MIE**  |

However the coded PoR in the [RTL](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cve2/blob/b8c94a3e84087e230581fcdddadbea398ea19a7e/rtl/cve2_cs_registers.sv#L745) is:
```
localparam status_t MSTATUS_RST_VAL = '{mie:  1'b0,
                                          mpie: 1'b1,
                                          mpp:  PRIV_LVL_U,
                                          mprv: 1'b0,
                                          tw:   1'b0};
```
Given that [PRIV_LVL_U](https://github.com/openhwgroup/cve2/blob/b8c94a3e84087e230581fcdddadbea398ea19a7e/rtl/cve2_pkg.sv#L206) is 2'b00, this yields a PoR of 0x0000_0080.

I believe that the documented PoR value is the proper one, but the coded PoR has been in the Ibex code for three years so I am not certain.

You can show this in simulation in CORE-V-VERIF by running the `debug_test`:
```
$ make test TEST=debug_test
```
(Set the SIMULATOR and USE_ISS vars as appropriate for your installation.)

title: When FS is 0 and a fld/fsd specific instruction causes an exception, there is a problem with the value of the mtval register
body:
**Describe the bug**

When the FS field in the mstatus register is 0, executing the `fld fa0, 288 (sp)` instruction causes an illegal instruction exception, and the values ​​of the xiangshan and nemu `mtval` registers are inconsistent.

Specifically, the value of the `xiangshan` mtval register is the machine code of the fld fa0, 288 (sp) instruction. 
The value of the mtval register in nemu is `0x00003512`

**To Reproduce**

```
.section .text
.globl _start
_start:
    li     t0, 0x8000000a00100a00     #FS: 00
    csrw    mstatus, t0 
    fld     fa0, 288(sp)
```

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/41eb772e-9dd9-476c-b786-7849024df991)

When I use spike for debugging, the instruction corresponding to `0x00003512` is `c.fldsp fa0, 288 (sp)`. After testing, the `fsd `command also has this situation

comments.body:
Thank you for your issue.
This is actually a bug in XiangShan.
The instruction `fld fa0, 288(sp)` was compiled into a compressed instruction `0x3512` under the C extension.
In XiangShan, the frontend decoding process expands the 16-bit C extension compressed instruction into a 32-bit instruction.
After that, it detects that FS is set to 0, so it stores the expanded instruction in mtval, rather than the original instruction itself.
This issue is currently being fixed by @sinceforYy

title: Possible bug in statistical corrector
body: ### Before start - [x] I have read the [RISC-V ISA Manual](https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual) and this is not a RISC-V ISA question. 我已经阅读过 RISC-V 指令集手册，这不是一个指令集本身的问题。 - [x] I have read the [XiangShan Documents](https://xiangshan-doc.readthedocs.io/zh_CN/latest). 我已经阅读过香山文档。 - [x] I have searched the previous issues and did not find anything relevant. 我已经搜索过之前的 issue，并没有找到相关的。 - [x] I have reviewed the commit messages from the relevant commit history. 我已经浏览过相关的提交历史和提交信息。 ### Describe the bug Hello, while inspecting code for the statistical corrector (SC.scala), I noticed a possible bug in the write conflict and forwarding mechanism. Background: When there is a read-write conflict to the table (read and write to the same index in the same cycle), the read takes priority, and the write data is instead saved to conflict_buffer until it can be written to the table in a later cycle. When there is a read to the same index while the conflict_buffer is valid (including the read of the original read-write conflict), then the read result is forwarded from the conflict_buffer, since the value in the table is stale. Problem: The table contains four ways per entry, but only one of the ways is changed during a write. So when forwarding from the conflict_buffer, we should expect that one of the ways is from the conflict_buffer, and the other three ways are from the table. However, it seems that in the current logic, when forwarding from the conflict_buffer, the other three ways are always zero. I also looked at a waveform from microbench to confirm this behavior. At marker 0: Read at index 84, the read result is {02, 05, 00, 00} At marker 1: Read-write conflict at index 84 way 1, the read result is {00, 06, 00 00} At marker 2: Read at index 84, the read result is {02, 06, 00, 00} -> I expected that the read result at marker 1 would be {02, 06, 00, 00}. However, since I am not very familiar with the XiangShan design, I am not sure whether this behavior will cause any issue downstream. If this is a real bug, I can try to write a fix. The conflict_buffer logic was added in #3671. Thanks, Sam ### Expected behavior During read-write conflict to the statistical corrector table, the read result should match the case where the write occurred before the read. In other words, the read result for the write way should be forwarded from the write data, and the read result for the other ways should be from the table. ### To Reproduce Steps: 1. Gather waveform for a workload with non-trivial branch activity, I used microbench from ready-to-run folder. 2. Locate read-write conflict to SC table with use_conflict_data signal in SCTable, the entry should also have more than one non-zero way. 3. Observe that the read result of the read-write conflict contains zero for all ways other than the write way. 4. Observe that reads to this index following the read-write conflict have the correct value. (The problem is only present during write forwarding.) ### Environment - XiangShan branch: master - XiangShan commit id: 977ac3b188267f31bfb32c7fa358f8b923a0e985 - NEMU commit id: N/A - SPIKE commit id: N/A ### Additional context _No response_

Hello, I'm looking into adding this function to the RAM wrapper now.

The current logic in SC blocks the RAM write during a conflict. However, at least for dual-port RAMs I have used in the past, this would not be necessary. When those RAMs received read and write at the same index, the write would still succeed, but the read result would be corrupt for ways that were written. In this case it is only necessary to bypass the write data, not block the write operation. It is better than the current logic, since the current logic may drop writes when there are back-to-back conflicting reads every cycle.

My question is, what is the required behavior for the dual-port RAM macros? Given that different RAM macros may have different behavior, it is a trade-off between performance and compatibility. I see three possible answers:
1. Simultaneous read and write to same index allowed, but read result is corrupt for ways that were written
2. Simultaneous read and write to same index allowed, but read result is corrupt for all ways
3. Simultaneous read and write to same index not allowed

From a design perspective, I would like to assume (1), since this is best for performance, and RAM macros I used in the past support this. But it would also be possible to make this configurable, in case a future user of XiangShan cannot use RAM macros with this behavior. Please let me know what the preferred choice is for XiangShan. title: [BUG] UnalignQueue "enqPtr < deqPtr" assertion triggered by cross-16B sd under sbuffer-stride pressure
body:
### Before start

- [x] I have read the [RISC-V ISA Manual](https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual) and this is not a RISC-V ISA question. 我已经阅读过 RISC-V 指令集手册，这不是一个指令集本身的问题。
- [x] I have read the [XiangShan Documents](https://xiangshan-doc.readthedocs.io/zh_CN/latest). 我已经阅读过香山文档。
- [x] I have searched the previous issues and did not find anything relevant. 我已经搜索过之前的 issue，并没有找到相关的。
- [x] I have reviewed the commit messages from the relevant commit history. 我已经浏览过相关的提交历史和提交信息。
- [x] I have reproduced the incorrect behaviors using the latest commit on the master branch. 我已经使用 master 分支最新的 commit 复现了不正确的行为。

### Branch

kunminghu-v3

### Describe the bug

A short loop of cross-16B `sd` stores with unique-line stride deterministically fires the assertion at `NewStoreQueue.scala:1414` inside the inner `UnalignQueue` module:

```scala
XSError(enqPtr < deqPtr && !full, s"Something wrong in UnalignQueue!")
```

```
[0] %Error: UnalignQueue.sv:139: Assertion failed in
    TOP.SimTop.cpu.l_soc.core_with_l2.core.memBlock.inner_lsq.storeQueue.unalignQueue:
    Assertion failed at LogUtils.scala:132
%Error: build/rtl/UnalignQueue.sv:139: Verilog $stop
Aborting...
```

The reproducer (200 iterations, two cross-16B `sd`s per iteration, 32-byte stride) fires the assertion deterministically within 5,000 cycles (5/5 reruns). Halving the iteration count, removing the stride, removing the second `sd`, or aligning the base address each makes the assertion not fire in the same cycle window.

### Expected behavior

`UnalignQueue` should maintain its `enqPtr` / `deqPtr` invariant under any legal sequence of cross-16B stores, regardless of sbuffer occupancy or loop-trip count.

### Environment

- Hardware
  - CPU: Intel Xeon Platinum 8592+
  - Memory (GB): 1006
  - Storage (GB): 2000
- Software
  - Operating system: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS
  - gcc version: 13.2.0
  - clang version: -
  - java version: openjdk 21.0.10
  - mill version: 0.12.15
- Repo
  - XiangShan commit id: `cc942e98c8fdd4b0ad3a8bddc9bfbd125b1f5d81`
  - difftest commit id: `f9d0bb858c18133984a5efd476f59989c69cb23f`
  - NEMU commit id: not used (`--no-diff`)
  - SPIKE commit id: not used
- Build & Run
  - Build command: `make sim-verilog && make -C ./difftest emu NUM_CORES=1 RTL_SUFFIX=sv`
  - Run command: `./build/verilator-compile/emu --no-diff -i unalignq_enqptr_deqptr.bin -C 5000`

### To Reproduce

Run the attached binary:

```
./build/verilator-compile/emu --no-diff -i unalignq_enqptr_deqptr.bin -C 5000
```

The assertion fires deterministically before 5,000 cycles (5/5 reruns).

The full reproducer is 9 instructions:

```assembly
_start:
  li   s2, 200                  # iteration count
  li   t0, 0x8010000F           # base; offset 15 -> cross-16B sd
  li   t3, 0xDEADBEEF
  li   t5, 32                   # unique-line stride
.Lloop:
  sd   t3, 0(t0)                # first  cross-16B sd
  sd   t3, 16(t0)               # second cross-16B sd
  add  t0, t0, t5
  addi s2, s2, -1
  bnez s2, .Lloop
```

To rebuild from the attached `.S`:

```bash
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc -nostdlib -nostartfiles -static \
    -march=rv64g -mabi=lp64 -T link.ld \
    -o unalignq_enqptr_deqptr.elf unalignq_enqptr_deqptr.S
riscv64-unknown-elf-objcopy -O binary unalignq_enqptr_deqptr.elf unalignq_enqptr_deqptr.bin
```

`link.ld` is a one-line linker script placing `.text` at `0x80000000`.

[unalignq_enqptr_deqptr.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27475354/unalignq_enqptr_deqptr.zip) — contains the `.S`, the pre-built `.bin`, the linker script, and the failing run log.

### Additional context

_No response_

title: StoreQueue cross-16B multi-match partial forward is treated as safe full overlap
body: ### Before start - [x] I have read the [RISC-V ISA Manual](https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual) and this is not a RISC-V ISA question. 我已经阅读过 RISC-V 指令集手册，这不是一个指令集本身的问题。 - [x] I have read the [XiangShan Documents](https://xiangshan-doc.readthedocs.io/zh_CN/latest). 我已经阅读过香山文档。 - [x] I have searched the previous issues and did not find anything relevant. 我已经搜索过之前的 issue，并没有找到相关的。 - [x] I have reviewed the commit messages from the relevant commit history. 我已经浏览过相关的提交历史和提交信息。 - [x] I have reproduced the incorrect behaviors using the latest commit on the master branch. 我已经使用 master 分支最新的 commit 复现了不正确的行为。 ### Branch kunminghu-v3 ### Describe the bug The StoreQueue forward path can accept a cross-16B partial store-to-load forward as a safe full-overlap forward when the load has multiple matching in-flight stores. The minimal sequence is: ```asm sd zero, 0(t0) sd zero, 8(t0) sd zero, 16(t0) sd zero, 24(t0) fence rw, rw li t1, 0xaabbccdd sw t1, 20(t0) # older store: bytes 20..23 li t2, 0x1122334455667788 sd t2, 12(t0) # younger store: bytes 12..19, crosses the 16B boundary ld a0, 16(t0) # load bytes 16..23 li t3, 0xaabbccdd11223344 bne a0, t3, fail ``` For the `ld a0, 16(t0)`, sequential semantics require: ```text bytes 16..19: from the younger sd 12(t0) = 0x11223344 bytes 20..23: from the older sw 20(t0) = 0xaabbccdd expected a0 = 0xaabbccdd11223344 ``` The reproduced XiangShan run instead writes back: ```text actual a0 = 0x0000000011223344 ``` The target load's memory address is `0x800000d0` (`test_area + 16`). The load instruction PC is `0x80000054`. Affected code path: ```scala // src/main/scala/xiangshan/mem/lsqueue/NewStoreQueue.scala val s2OutMask = ParallelLookUp(s2ByteSelectOffset, s2SelectMask) & s2LoadMaskEnd val s2FullOverlap = (s2SelectDataEntry.byteMask & s2LoadMaskEnd) === s2LoadMaskEnd val s2SafeForward = !s2MultiMatch || s2FullOverlap s2Resp.bits.forwardInvalid := !s2SafeForward || s2Cross4KPage ``` `s2OutMask` is the selected store byte mask after rotation into the load coordinate system. In the failing case it is `0x000f`, so only the low four bytes of the 8-byte load are actually forwarded. However, `s2FullOverlap` compares the unrotated selected-store `byteMask` against `s2LoadMaskEnd`. For this cross-16B case, that unrotated comparison reports full overlap even though the rotated forward mask only covers half of the load. Consequently, `s2SafeForward` is asserted and `forwardInvalid` remains low, so the load is not replayed. The current configuration makes this a real path, not an artificial configuration mismatch: * `XSCoreParameters.VLEN = 128`, so StoreQueue forwarding uses a 16-byte (`VLEN/8`) coordinate. * `SQDataEntryBundle.byteMask` is `(VLEN/8).W`. * `TLMinimalConfig` has `StoreQueueForwardWithMask = true`. * `NewStoreQueue.scala` explicitly handles `cross16Byte`, `s1Next16BMatchVec`, `s2ByteSelectOffset`, and rotated forward data/masks. ### Expected behavior For a multi-match load, if the selected youngest store only covers part of the load after rotation into the load coordinate system, StoreQueue must not treat the forward as safe. It should replay the load or otherwise ensure that all bytes are supplied according to store age order. In this PoC, the expected architectural value for `ld a0, 16(t0)` is: ```text a0 = 0xaabbccdd11223344 ``` StoreQueue should not allow: ```text s2MultiMatch = 1 s2LoadMaskEnd = 0x00ff s2OutMask = 0x000f s2SafeForward = 1 forwardInvalid = 0 ``` because this combination means the load needs 8 bytes, only 4 bytes are forwarded, another matching store exists, and yet the load is allowed to consume the partial result. ### Environment * Software * RISC-V GCC used for the PoC workload: `riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc 15.1.0` * XiangShan checkout HEAD: `3931c5112c528299a23c256bdd77fb90813afa6e` ### To Reproduce The attachment [xiangshan-sq-cross16-forward-poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28091274/xiangshan-sq-cross16-forward-poc.zip) contains: 1. `cross16_multistore_forward.S`: minimal bare-metal PoC. 2. `cross16_stale_secret_forward.S`: variant that initializes old memory bytes to `0xdeadbeef` to demonstrate stale-data exposure. 3. `link.ld`: linker script placing `_start` at `0x80000000`. 4. `parse_cross16_vcd.py` and `parse_cross16_secret_vcd.py`: VCD monitors for the main and stale-data variants. 5. `monitor_repro_0_11550.json` and `monitor_secret_0_11700.json`: reproduced monitor results. 6. `cross16_repro_hier_16740_16770.{vcd,fst}` and `cross16_secret_hier_16738_16768.{vcd,fst}`: small hierarchy-preserving waveforms containing the relevant SQ/writeback signals around the failing event. 7. `run_repro_0_11550.log` and `run_secret_0_11700.log`: emulator logs. Build the main PoC: ```bash riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc \ -nostdlib -nostartfiles \ -march=rv64gc_zicsr_zifencei -mabi=lp64 \ -T link.ld \ -o cross16_multistore_forward.elf \ cross16_multistore_forward.S riscv64-unknown-elf-objcopy \ -O binary \ cross16_multistore_forward.elf \ cross16_multistore_forward.bin riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump \ -dr cross16_multistore_forward.elf \ > cross16_multistore_forward.objdump ``` Run the waveform-enabled XiangShan emulator: ```bash emu \ -C 11550 -b 0 -e 11550 \ -i cross16_multistore_forward.bin \ --no-diff \ --dump-wave-full \ --wave-path=cross16_repro_0_11550.vcd \ --force-dump-result \ > run_repro_0_11550.log 2>&1 ``` Parse the VCD: ```bash python3 parse_cross16_vcd.py \ cross16_repro_0_11550.vcd \ --json-out monitor_repro_0_11550.json \ > monitor_repro_0_11550.log 2>&1 ``` The reproduced result is: ```text predicate_result = reproduced expected_load_data = 0xaabbccdd11223344 bad_writebacks = 0x0000000011223344, 0x0000000011223344 good_writebacks = [] ``` At VCD time `16758`, the StoreQueue monitor sees: ```text s2Valid = 1 s2Resp_valid = 1 s2ForwardValid = 1 s2MultiMatch = 1 s2LoadMaskEnd = 0x00ff s2OutMask = 0x000f s2SafeForward = 1 forwardInvalid = 0 s2LoadPaddr = 0x800000d s2LoadStart = 0 ``` At VCD time `16760`, integer writeback port 0 writes: ```text toIntRf_valid = 1 toIntRf_bits_isFromLoadUnit = 1 toIntRf_bits_pdest = 0x0f toIntRf_bits_data = 0x0000000011223344 toRob_bits_debugInfo_vaddr = 0x800000d0 toRob_bits_debugInfo_paddr = 0x800000d0 ``` This connects the StoreQueue partial-forward decision to an architectural integer-register writeback for the target load. ### Additional context The stale-data variant changes only the initial bytes at `test_area + 16` before the older `sw`: ```asm li t4, 0xdeadbeefcafebabe sd t4, 16(t0) ... sw t1, 20(t0) sd t2, 12(t0) ld a0, 16(t0) ``` Sequential semantics still require: ```text a0 = 0xaabbccdd11223344 ``` The reproduced stale-data variant instead writes back: ```text a0 = 0xdeadbeef11223344 ``` The stale high 32 bits should have been overwritten by the older `sw 20(t0)`. This shows that the bug can expose stale bytes architecturally when software relies on an in-flight store to overwrite previous memory contents. This is not a branch-prediction or Spectre-style transient-execution issue. It is an out-of-order load/store forwarding correctness bug in the speculative memory-execution machinery. The incorrect value is not merely transient; it reaches integer-register writeback and changes the architectural path (`bne a0, t3, fail`). In principle, Spike/NEMU difftest should also catch this: Spike executes the sequence sequentially and obtains `a0 = 0xaabbccdd11223344`, while the reproduced XiangShan run writes `a0 = 0x0000000011223344`. In this workspace, the available `build_vcd/emu` was used with `--no-diff` for waveform evidence; passing `--diff` to this particular binary prints the help text and exits, so I used VCD-based validation instead.
